extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors, litigators, and patent examiners working on software/computer-related patents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practice tips for analyzing and drafting software- and computer-related patent claims for subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (Alice/Mayo framework). Emphasizes distinguishing abstract ideas from technical solutions and drafting/specification strategies to survive eligibility challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/tangible form requirement for non-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: "For all categories except process claims, the eligible subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form." (Digitech cited)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claimed invention is not a 'concrete thing,' 'tangible article,' or combination of substances, it may fail §101. Use physical or tangible implementation language where appropriate; be cautious when claims only define abstract systems (e.g., symbol systems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that merely define symbols/definitions are not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: What is claimed is not a physical or tangible thing and not a process as things are simply being defined and not acted upon (e.g., phonetic symbol system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider claiming practical applications, transformations, or operations of the symbol system rather than only definitions. Query whether storing on a storage device changes eligibility (risk: printed matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data recitations require actionable effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of a claim that recite data is not given weight unless that data can act upon something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mere recitation of data; claim data that 'result or causes something to happen or be controlled.' Be cautious claiming monetary data. If you must claim data, tie it to operations, control, or physical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed-matter/storage recitation caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Query whether claiming it as stored on a storage device would make it eligible. Might be rejected as mere printed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely reciting storage of data on a medium may not overcome §101 rejections; tie storage to functional interaction or processing that alters behavior or causes action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea when result-oriented without technical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract idea was found because the claims were result oriented, without technical detail. (Interval Licensing)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that are phrased as desired outcomes or high-level results, without specific technical means, risk being characterized as abstract ideas. Include technical detail and mechanisms in claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on technical solutions/improvements for UI inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should focus on technical solutions, technical improvements or improved functionality for user-interface based inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For UI inventions, draft claims and spec to show how the UI change improves system functionality or technical operation (not merely aesthetics or presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed or efficiency alone does not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Just because a computer can do something faster does not transform the invention into something eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize a technical solution to a technical problem rather than mere performance gains. Show how speed is achieved by a specific technical means rather than asserted at a high level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly broad claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful seeking an overly broad interpretation of your claims; broad interpretations can import prior art and make the claim appear abstract or preemptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue for claim constructions that highlight the claimed technical features; use specification support to constrain claim meaning where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue non-preemption when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Assert that the claims do not preempt all use of the claimed abstract idea; distinguish prior cases by showing narrower scope or specific technical means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize claim limitations that leave other approaches open; use arguments about non-preemption as part of Alice Step 1/Step 2 analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage the specification to show the technical problem and solution
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion leans heavily on the specification for identifying the problem and ensuring the solution is in the claims. (KPN, SRI, Packet Intelligence)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the specification to describe the technical problem, explain why it is technical, and detail the specific technical means used to solve it. Use intrinsic evidence to support claim construction and eligibility arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to a non-abstract technological improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be patent-eligible under Alice Step 1 if they are directed to a non-abstract improvement in an existing technological process (e.g., improved error checking in data transmission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the claims as improvements to technology (specific methods/devices) and show how the claimed limitations provide a technical benefit or improvement over prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft dependent claims to delineate specific solution when independent claim is broad
rubrics_metrics.description: If the client wants a broader independent claim, ensure there are dependent claims that clearly delineate the specific solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include dependent claims that recite specific implementations, parameters, and mechanisms so that a court can point to concrete claim language if a broad independent claim is challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claims: non-preemption vs enablement/written-description risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Genus claims may avoid preemption and thus pass §101, but may implicate enablement and written description issues under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If drafting broad 'genus' claims, ensure the specification supports and enables the full breadth claimed to mitigate §112 risk even if §101 is satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not oversimplify claim language in eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must be careful to avoid oversimplifying the claims by looking at them generally and failing to account for the specific requirements of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing eligibility, focus on the precise claim limitations and how they constrain the invention; avoid reducing claims to an overly abstract characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express technical problem/solution in both spec and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting a 'technological solution to a technological problem' in the specification is valuable; the specification bolsters conclusions that claims are directed to a technological solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the technical shortcomings of prior art, articulate the concrete technical improvements provided by the invention, and mirror those aspects in claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim specific means of achieving the asserted technical result
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure that the specific aspects of how to achieve the technical solution are claimed — relying solely on the specification may be insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete components, data structures, algorithms, or processing steps in claims, not just a description in the spec, so the claims themselves recite the 'how.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about heavy reliance on the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is being more heavily relied on for determining patent eligibility under §101; however, courts differ on whether reliance on the spec vs claim language is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specification to support and construe claim terms, but ensure claims stand on their own by reciting tangible technical features and steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical aspect alone insufficient to avoid abstract-idea finding
rubrics_metrics.description: The physicality of items involved (e.g., paper checks being processed and transported) is not by itself enough to exempt claims from being directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that claimed physical steps change how computers operate or materially improve data capture/processing; avoid merely adding conventional physical actions as token 'physical' elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize interruption of preemption through claim limitations and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that avoid preempting all approaches to an abstract idea (e.g., by specifying limitations or alternatives) are less likely to be invalid under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to include concrete, limiting features (e.g., specific data manipulations, timing/permutation techniques, tables) and identify alternative approaches left open by the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming monetary/data-only schemes without technical tie
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to monetary schemes or purely transactional data processing (e.g., early crediting of merchant accounts) are likely to be characterized as abstract unless tied to technical improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention involves financial/data processing, tie it explicitly to technical improvements in data capture, transmission, verification, or processing mechanisms.
